title: Users Don't Care About Your Figma File
intro: Clean, modern interfaces fail every day because teams skip basic usability principles. Visual polish doesn't make a product usable. Clarity is not a luxury — it's the foundation of UX.

learn.title: Polish ≠ usability
learn.text:
A product can look polished while failing users. Clean design isn't useful if users can't figure out how to use it.

Teams spend weeks perfecting spacing, color systems, and component libraries. The Figma file looks immaculate. Then users:

→ Can't find the button they need
→ Don't understand what an icon means
→ Submit a form and get no confirmation
→ Hit 'Archive' when they meant 'Add'

**The rule:** Make things that work first. Then make them look good.

UX quality is judged by whether users can complete real tasks confidently, not by how good the interface looks.

right.label: UX quality (users)
items: Can I find what I need?
Do I understand what this does?
Do I know what just happened?

try.q: A design review praises a settings page for its 'clean, minimal layout.' Users in testing can't find the save button. What's the real quality?
options: High internal quality, low UX quality — it looks good but doesn't work
Low quality overall — the design is bad
High quality — users will learn eventually
It needs more user education, not redesign
try.explain: The Figma file is great. The UX isn't. These are different things, and only one of them matters to users.

learn.title: The five failure patterns
learn.text:
**1. Lack of clarity** — Unlabeled icons, hidden requirements, controls that change names or locations. Password rules hidden behind an info icon that only appear after submission fails.

**2. Small interaction problems** — Tiny click targets, buttons with no visual feedback, clickable-looking elements that aren't clickable.

**3. Communication failures** — No confirmation after submissions. Vague error messages. A budget tool where users resubmitted because nothing said the first one went through.

**4. Cognitive load** — Modals that hide context users need. Forms that force you to remember rules or re-enter data.

**5. Dangerous neighbors** — Destructive actions placed next to common ones. 'Archive Project' next to 'Add Task,' both looking identical.

try.q: A cloud storage app updates its layout. Users can't find the share button because the icon changed position and has no label. Which failure pattern?
options: Lack of clarity — unlabeled icons that break muscle memory
Cognitive load — too many features
Communication failure — no feedback
Dangerous neighbors — misplaced actions
try.explain: Unlabeled icons + changed position = clarity failure. Users relied on location AND label, and both were taken away.

learn.title: Measure task completion, not aesthetics
learn.text:
The real test of UX quality: **Can users complete their actual tasks?**

**Measure these:**
→ Task completion rate
→ Time on task
→ Error rate
→ Recovery from errors
→ Confidence level (do they know it worked?)

**Not these (as quality metrics):**
→ Visual consistency score
→ Component coverage
→ Design system compliance
→ Stakeholder approval in review

Design reviews catch visual problems. Usability tests catch task problems. You need both, but if you skip one, skip the design review.

**Watch for the "build trap"** (Torres/Perri): Teams obsess over shipping features and assume success = launches. But customers don't care about your feature count. They care about solving their problems. Measure outcomes (did the user succeed?) not outputs (did we ship it?).

**The bottom line:** Clarity is not a luxury. It is the foundation of UX.

try.q: Your design system has 98% component coverage. Users complete the core task only 60% of the time. What's the priority?
options: Fix the task completion problem — that's what users experience
Increase component coverage to 100%
Both are equally important
Run a design review to find visual inconsistencies
try.explain: Users don't care about your component library. They care about whether they can do what they came to do.

test.q: What does 'Users don't care about your Figma file' mean?
options: Internal design quality (polish, consistency) is different from UX quality (can users do their tasks)
Figma is a bad tool
Users don't look at design files
Visual design doesn't matter at all
test.explain: The Figma file serves the team. UX quality serves the user. A perfect file doesn't guarantee a usable product.

test.q: A form submission has no confirmation message. Users resubmit, creating duplicates. Which failure pattern?
options: Communication failure — no feedback after action
Cognitive load — too complex
Dangerous neighbors — wrong button
Lack of clarity — unclear labels
test.explain: Users need to know what happened. Silent submissions cause resubmissions and erode trust.

test.q: Why are 'dangerous neighbors' a UX problem?
options: Placing destructive actions next to common ones leads to accidental data loss
They make the interface look cluttered
They violate design system guidelines
They slow down page performance
test.explain: 'Archive Project' next to 'Add Task' — same size, same style, adjacent. One click and your project is gone.

test.q: Which is a better measure of UX quality?
options: Task completion rate
Design system compliance
Number of components used
Stakeholder approval in design review
test.explain: Task completion rate directly measures whether users can do what they came to do. Everything else is internal.

test.q: What's the right order of priorities?
options: Make it work, then make it look good
Make it look good, then make it work
Make it look good — usability follows naturally
They should happen simultaneously with equal weight
test.explain: Clarity is the foundation. Polish is the finish. A beautiful product that doesn't work is worse than an ugly one that does.
